lessons.title: Why this works
lessons.body:
Your brain is not bad at remembering — it's bad at remembering the kind of information school and work throw at it: abstract, unordered, and boring. What it's extremely good at is remembering places, faces, stories, and anything vivid or emotional. Every technique in this app is really one move: turn the boring thing into a vivid thing, then give the vivid thing an address.

Kevin Horsley, in [i]Unlimited Memory[/i], compresses the whole discipline into a loop he calls the four C's: [b]Concentrate[/b] on the information fully before trying to encode it, [b]Create[/b] a vivid image for it, [b]Connect[/b] that image to something you already know (a place, a peg, another image), and use it through [b]Continuous[/b] review so it survives past the next hour. Skip Concentrate and the image is fuzzy from the start. Skip Connect and you have a vivid image with no way back to it. Every lesson from here is a way of doing Create and Connect well.

lessons.title: The SEE principle
lessons.tryLabel: Try it on your own text
lessons.body:
An image only sticks if it's memorable, and "memorable" is not automatic — you have to build it. Horsley's SEE principle is the checklist:

[b]Senses[/b] — don't just picture it, put sound, texture, smell, even taste into the scene. A silent, still image fades; a scene you can hear and feel doesn't.
[b]Exaggeration[/b] — make it absurdly big, absurdly small, or absurdly wrong. A normal apple on a table is forgettable; an apple the size of a car crashing through your ceiling is not.
[b]Energize[/b] — add motion. A static object is easy to skip over; something exploding, spinning, or chasing you demands attention.

Try it: take the word "invoice" — dull, abstract. SEE version: a giant invoice unrolls like a scroll, catches fire, and the smoke smells like burnt paper as it screams numbers at you. That's absurd on purpose. Absurd is what survives.

lessons.title: Concentration comes first
lessons.body:
Horsley is blunt about this in [i]Unlimited Memory[/i]: image-building techniques only work on information you actually attended to. A brilliant SEE image built on a half-heard fact is a brilliant image of the wrong fact.

Before you memorize anything — a deck of cards, a page of a book, a person's name — give yourself two or three seconds of nothing else: no phone, no scrolling, no half-listening. Horsley frames concentration as a trainable habit, not a fixed trait; the more you practice giving something your full attention before encoding it, the shorter that runway gets. In competition terms, this is your pre-round routine — the few seconds where you consciously arrive before the clock starts.

lessons.title: The memory palace, and Horsley's Car Method
lessons.body:
The method of loci — Latin for "places" — is the oldest memory technique on record, used by Greek and Roman orators to deliver hour-long speeches without notes. The idea: pick a route through a place you know cold, break it into a fixed sequence of distinct stations, and mentally "place" one vivid image at each station as you walk through it. To recall, you walk the same route again in your head and pick up what you left at each stop.

Horsley teaches a compact version of this he calls the [b]Car Method[/b]: use your own car — bonnet, wing mirror, steering wheel, gear stick, glovebox, back seat — as a small, always-available palace when you don't want to build a whole building from scratch. Same principle, smaller scale.

What makes a good palace, either way: stations you can picture instantly without effort, a route you always walk the same direction, and enough distance between stations that two images don't blur into one.

lessons.title: The empty run: familiarize before you encode
lessons.tryLabel: Take an empty walk through the castle
lessons.body:
Before you place a single item, walk the space with no job to do. This is the step most beginners skip, and skipping it is why a hastily-adopted palace falls apart under pressure: if you're still half-figuring out where the door is while also trying to encode a fact there, both processes compete and both lose.

Give any new palace one pass where the only goal is to notice it — walk the route, name each station out loud, notice what's actually distinctive about each one. Only once the layout feels boring and automatic should you start hanging images on it. If you're using this app's castle as a palace, walk all eight rooms once before placing anything: follow the glowing arrow, open the map with M, get properly lost and then found. This is well-established spatial-memory principle rather than something I've traced to Horsley's own material specifically.

lessons.title: Placing information with SEE
lessons.tryLabel: Open a palace and try it
lessons.body:
Building a palace and filling it are two different skills — this lesson is the second one. At each station, don't just "put" the information there; build a full SEE-image where the station itself is part of the scene.

If your third station is "kitchen counter" and the fact is "the meeting moved to Thursday," don't picture a sticky note that says Thursday — picture a giant number 4 wearing a chef's hat, deep-frying your kitchen counter, and the smoke alarm is going off. Loud, moving, ridiculous, anchored to a place you already know. Do this station by station, in order, and you're not memorizing a list anymore — you're remembering a walk you took.

lessons.title: Chaining: the linking method
lessons.body:
Not everything needs a building. For a short list — five to ten items — Horsley's linking (or narrative) technique skips the palace entirely: you chain each image directly into the next one in a continuous, absurd mini-story. Item one interacts with item two, item two interacts with item three, and so on, so recalling item one automatically drags item two into view.

Say your list is candle, elephant, umbrella: a candle melts onto an elephant's back, the elephant sneezes so hard it launches into the air holding an umbrella like a parachute. One flowing scene, not three separate facts. This is faster to set up than a palace and works well for quick lists or a short set of talking points — but it's more fragile than a palace over long sequences, since one broken link can knock out everything after it. Use a palace when order matters over a long stretch; use linking for something short and disposable.

lessons.title: The peg / rhyme technique
lessons.body:
A peg system is a fixed, pre-memorized set of images — usually attached to numbers — that you reuse over and over as hooks for new information, the same way you'd reuse a set of coat hooks. Horsley teaches a rhyme-based version: each number 1 through 10 gets a word that rhymes with it, turned into a picture. A common version: 1-bun, 2-shoe, 3-tree, 4-door, 5-hive, 6-sticks, 7-heaven, 8-gate, 9-wine, 10-hen.

Once those ten pegs are solid — and they only take an evening to learn — memorizing "the fourth item is a stapler" becomes "a door made of staplers," instantly. Unlike a palace, you don't need to invent a route; the pegs are already there, in order, permanently. Good for short numbered lists, agenda items, or anything you want random access to (jump straight to item 7 without walking the whole sequence).

lessons.title: The body technique
lessons.body:
The most portable peg system you own is your own body. Pick ten fixed points in sequence — feet, knees, hips, stomach, chest, shoulders, neck, mouth, eyes, top of head — and use them exactly like palace stations: one vivid image hung on each, in order.

Because you're never without your body, this system travels anywhere a physical palace can't — useful for memorizing something on the spot, mid-conversation, with nothing to write on. It has the same limit as any short peg set: past ten or so items it gets crowded, so it's best for short, immediate lists rather than long-form material.

lessons.title: Number systems for speed
lessons.body:
Rhyme pegs are great up to about ten items, but a memory-sport numbers event asks for dozens or hundreds of digits, and you can't rhyme your way to a hundred unique images fast enough. The tool competitive memorizers use instead is the [b]Major System[/b]: every digit 0–9 is mapped to a consonant sound (0=s/z, 1=t/d, 2=n, 3=m, 4=r, 5=l, 6=j/sh/ch, 7=k/g, 8=f/v, 9=p/b), vowels are free, and you convert pairs of digits into real words by their consonant sounds. "32" becomes m-n → "moon." "71" becomes k-t → "cat" or "kite." String the words into a scene at each palace station and you can encode two digits per image instead of one.

This is standard technique across the sport — I haven't been able to confirm it from Horsley's own material directly. If his book teaches a different number system, tell me and I'll fold it into this lesson properly. I've filled in a starting word for every pair from 00 to 99 below — replace any of them with your own (a name, a place, whatever's more vivid to you) and it's saved from then on.

lessons.title: Person-Action-Object (PAO)
lessons.body:
For playing cards — and for numbers once you're fast — most competitive memorizers use a system called PAO: every card (or every 2-digit number) is pre-assigned a Person, an Action, and an Object. The queen of spades might always be "a chef flipping a pancake." The real power shows up when you combine three cards into one image: card one supplies the Person, card two supplies the Action, card three supplies the Object — so instead of three separate images you get one scene ("the chef flips a pancake made of fire"), and you've compressed three cards into a single station.

Building a full 52-card PAO table is a project in itself — most people build it a handful of cards a week rather than all at once. Like the numbers system above, PAO is standard competitive-memory technique rather than something I can point to directly in Horsley's material — if you've got his approach to cards, send it over and I'll rewrite this properly. The builder below is empty on purpose: the whole point of PAO is that the people and actions are vivid [i]to you[/i], so there's nothing pre-filled to undo.

lessons.title: Building your table gradually
lessons.body:
Don't try to invent 52 Person-Action-Object images in one sitting — it doesn't stick and it isn't fun. A more realistic build: assign 4–6 cards a week, always to people and actions that are already vivid to you (real people you know well work better than invented characters), and drill only the cards you've assigned until they're automatic before adding more.

By the time you've built the full deck this way, the early cards are already fast, and you've avoided the trap of a table that's complete on paper but useless under time pressure.

lessons.title: Abstract words & sound-alikes
lessons.tryLabel: Try it on your own text
lessons.body:
Some words simply have no picture — names, jargon, abstract nouns. Horsley's fix, worked through in [i]Unlimited Memory[/i]: break the word into pieces that do sound like something, and picture those pieces instead. His own examples: "Washington" becomes "washing a tin," "hydrogen" becomes a fire hydrant drinking gin. Neither sounds elegant, and that's fine — you're not translating the word, you're building a scene your memory can hold, and you unpack it back into the original word on recall.

Try this on your own material: pick an abstract term from whatever you're studying, split it into syllables, and ask what each syllable sounds like as a real object. It gets faster with practice, and it's the single most useful skill for memorizing anything text-based — which is exactly what the Library tab is for. The Library can also suggest a first-draft SEE image for any passage you've pulled in, if you want a starting point.

lessons.title: Names & faces
lessons.body:
Names and faces fail for a specific, fixable reason: you meet the face and hear the name at the same moment, with nothing to link them. The fix is three steps. First, pick one distinctive feature on the face — a sharp jaw, heavy eyebrows, a gap in the teeth — something you could pick out of a lineup. Second, turn the name into a sound-alike image the way you would any abstract word. Third, place that image directly on the feature you picked, ideally doing something active to it.

"Nikhil" might become a needle ("nee–") pinning a chill (a shivering figure) — pinned right onto that sharp jawline. Reviewing the pairing once, a few seconds after you build it, roughly doubles how long it survives.

lessons.title: Presenting from memory: the FLOOR principle
lessons.body:
A side benefit of these techniques, and one Horsley spends real time on: speaking or presenting without notes. His FLOOR principle names what an audience actually retains from any talk, whether the speaker meant them to or not: [b]F[/b]irst things (the opening), [b]L[/b]ast things (the close), [b]O[/b]utstanding information (whatever was most vivid or surprising), [b]O[/b]wn links (whatever the listener personally connected to), and [b]R[/b]epeated information (whatever you said more than once).

Structuring a presentation deliberately around FLOOR — a strong open, a strong close, one deliberately vivid moment, and one point repeated on purpose — does double duty: the talk lands better for the audience, and because you built it around a small number of vivid anchors rather than a wall of text, it's far easier for you to hold the whole thing in memory and deliver it without a script.

lessons.title: Memorizing books & long text: beyond one-shot recall
lessons.body:
Everything up to here is optimized for one-shot recall: memorize it once, recite it once, done — that's what a competition rewards. Remembering a book, or a set of sayings you actually want to carry with you for years, is a different goal, and it needs one more ingredient on top of imagery: [b]spaced review[/b]. An image you never revisit fades like anything else; the same image reviewed at increasing intervals — say a day later, three days later, a week later, three weeks later — moves into long-term memory and stays there with less and less effort each time.

This is why the Library tab's "Practice recall" exists separately from a one-off palace walk: it's built for exactly this repeated-review loop. Extract the passages you care about, place the important ones in a palace using SEE and sound-alikes, and then come back on a rough schedule rather than once. The techniques get it in; review is what keeps it in.

lessons.title: Warm-up & state
lessons.body: Horsley's concentration point from Level 1 applies with extra force right before a timed drill: a scattered thirty seconds at the start of a memorize phase costs you disproportionately, because everything that follows is trying to catch up. A short settle routine before you hit start — a few slow breaths, one conscious moment of "I'm doing this now, nothing else" — costs almost nothing and measurably steadies the first few images, which are usually the ones that carry the most weight for scoring (this app's "correct run from the start" stat rewards exactly that).

lessons.title: Pacing & palace hygiene
lessons.body:
Two practical habits that separate steady scores from wildly inconsistent ones. First, pacing: if one image isn't forming cleanly, don't stall on it — place whatever half-formed version you have and move on; a weak image beats a missing one, and a missing one is far cheaper than the three seconds you'd lose trying to perfect it.

Second, palace hygiene: reusing the same palace for a new drill without clearing it mentally causes old and new images to blur together — what memory athletes sometimes call interference. Before reusing a palace, take a few seconds to consciously picture it empty, or keep a rotation of two or three palaces per discipline so each one gets a rest before you come back to it. This one is general competitive-memory practice rather than something I can trace to Horsley directly.
